---
name: keyshroud
description: Use secrets (API keys, tokens, passwords) from the user's keyshroud vault (an encrypted local vault, or their Vaultwarden/Bitwarden) without ever seeing their values. Use whenever a command needs a credential, the user mentions a token/API key/.env, asks to store or rotate a secret, or output might contain a secret.
---

# keyshroud

The user's secrets live in keyshroud's encrypted local vault, or in their
Vaultwarden/Bitwarden (`keyshroud status` says which). You work with **names and
references**, never values. keyshroud injects values into child processes and replaces them
in output with `<redacted:NAME>`.

## Rules

1. Never ask the user to paste a secret into the chat. To store one, run this
   yourself; it opens a hidden-input dialog on the user's desktop, and you only
   see `created … verified=yes`:
   ```bash
   keyshroud add --env STRIPE_API_KEY --item "Stripe API key" --notes "billing service"
   ```
   Tell the user a dialog is waiting for them, and ask for one secret at a time;
   if they cancel, do not ask again unprompted. Never ask for the vault master
   password or passphrase. With the MCP server, call `secrets_request` instead. Over SSH or without a display there is no dialog:
   then give the user the command to run in their own terminal.
2. Never print, echo, `cat`, base64, or otherwise transform a secret value.
   `<redacted:NAME>` in output means the secret was used correctly. Do not try
   to recover it.
3. Never write a secret value into a file. Write a reference instead.
4. Run **every** command that uses a secret through `keyshroud run` (or the
   `secrets_run` MCP tool). Plain shell commands are only masked when they
   succeed; `keyshroud run` masks even when the command fails.
5. Never run `keyshroud get`, `keyshroud env --shell`, `keyshroud inject`
   without `-o`, or `bw` directly — they print values.

## See what exists

```bash
keyshroud env            # wired names only
keyshroud doctor         # vault, keychain, and wiring state (no values)
```
MCP: `secrets_list`, `vault_status`.

## Run a command that needs a secret

```bash
keyshroud run -- gh pr list                       # all wired secrets as env vars
keyshroud run --only GH_TOKEN -- gh pr list       # least privilege
keyshroud run --env-file .env.refs -- npm test    # project references
```
Inside the command, refer to `$GH_TOKEN`; keyshroud resolves it. Output is
masked automatically when not attached to a terminal. MCP: `secrets_run`.

## References (safe to commit)

```
keyshroud://<item>              value in the local vault (also: /notes, /id)
bw://<item>                 Vaultwarden login password
bw://<item>/username        also: notes, totp, uri, id
bw://<item>/fields/<name>   custom field
```
Percent-encode `/` in item names (`keyshroud://a%2Fb`). A project's `.env.refs`:
```dotenv
GH_TOKEN=keyshroud://GitHub CLI token
DATABASE_URL=bw://Prod DB/fields/url
LOG_LEVEL=debug
```

Config files that cannot read env vars: `keyshroud inject -i config.tpl -o config`
renders `{{ keyshroud://item }}` and `{{ bw://item/field }}` placeholders into a 0600 file. Add the output to
`.gitignore`.

## Before committing

```bash
keyshroud scan .          # exits 1 and lists file:line NAME for each vault value it finds
```

## Exit codes

`0` ok · `2` usage · `3` vault locked/unavailable (ask the user to run
`keyshroud unlock`) · `4` secret missing or item name ambiguous · `5` would
overwrite existing state.

When the vault is locked, a command waits while a dialog on the user's desktop
asks for the master password or passphrase. Never ask for it in chat and never
retry in a loop after a cancel. A local vault that needs a passphrase and does
not exist yet is created by the user in a terminal (`keyshroud unlock`).

On a Mac with a Touch ID vault, a command that needs a secret shows a Touch ID sheet. If an error says
the vault "opens with Touch ID at the Mac", tell the user to approve the sheet, or to run
`keyshroud unlock` at the Mac; never retry in a loop. `keyshroud list` shows item names and their
wiring. Never run `keyshroud rm --yes` or `keyshroud rekey` on your own: they delete or re-key the
user's vault, so only run them when the user asks.

`migrate` is for Vaultwarden users: it needs the personal vault. You may start `setup --email`;
the user picks the agent account's password on the signup page, never through you. If an item
is missing after `setup`, ask the user to run `keyshroud migrate --item "NAME"`.

**Your agents use the keys. They never see them.** **Keep API keys out of Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Cline, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, pi and omp** — secrets stay in an encrypted vault on your machine (or in your own [Vaultwarden](https://github.com/dani-garcia/vaultwarden) or Bitwarden, to share them between machines), and every value is masked before the model reads it. [![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/keyshroud.svg)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/keyshroud) [![Downloads](https://img.shields.io/npm/dm/keyshroud.svg)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/keyshroud) [![CI](https://github.com/dinhkarate/keyshroud/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/dinhkarate/keyshroud/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg)](LICENSE) [![Node](https://img.shields.io/node/v/keyshroud.svg)](package.json) [🚀 Quickstart](#quickstart) · [🔐 Local vault](#the-local-vault) · [🔄 Sync with Vaultwarden](#sync-across-machines-vaultwarden-or-bitwarden) · [🔌 Supported agents](#supported-agents) · [⚙️ How it works](#how-it-works) · [❓ FAQ](#faq) · [🛡️ Security model](#security-model) · [🌐 Website](https://keyshroud.dev) [🇻🇳 Tiếng Việt](i18n/README.vi.md) · [🇨🇳 简体中文](i18n/README.zh-CN.md) · [🇯🇵 日本語](i18n/README.ja-JP.md)

```console $ keyshroud run --mask -- sh -c 'echo "deploying with $GH_TOKEN"; gh api user -q .login' deploying with dinhkarate ``` The command got the real token. The transcript — and the model reading it — got ``. (Masking is automatic when an agent runs the command; `--mask` forces it in a human terminal.) ## Why keyshroud? Coding agents need credentials to do real work: `gh`, `npm publish`, cloud CLIs, webhooks, databases. The usual options are bad: - ❌ **Paste the key into the chat** — now it is in the transcript, the provider's logs, and every future context window - ❌ **Put it in `.env`** — the agent `cat`s it while debugging, or commits it - ❌ **Pay for a secrets manager** — `op run` needs a 1Password subscription, and most "agent vaults" are hosted SaaS - ❌ **Use a vault MCP server** — most of them return the plaintext value straight to the model **keyshroud fixes this:** - ✅ **Names, not values** — agents see `GH_TOKEN` and `keyshroud://GitHub token`, never the token - ✅ **Masked output** — any value that reaches stdout/stderr becomes `` - ✅ **Nothing to set up** — an encrypted vault file with its key in your OS keychain; no account, no server - ✅ **Sync if you want it** — Vaultwarden on a $5 VPS or a Raspberry Pi, or Bitwarden, for several machines - ✅ **Free** — MIT-licensed, no telemetry ## Features | | | |---|---| | 🙈 **Masked output** | `keyshroud run` replaces every secret value in stdout/stderr with `` — streaming-safe across chunk boundaries. | | 🔐 **Local vault** | An AES-256-GCM file whose key is in the macOS keychain, the Linux Secret Service or Windows DPAPI (a passphrase where there is none). No account, no server, no `bw`. | | 🪝 **Agent hooks** | The pi/omp `tool_result` hook redacts every tool result, failed ones included. Claude Code's `PostToolUse` hook redacts every *successful* tool result (Bash, Read, Grep, MCP…) — see [limits](#security-model). | | 🔌 **MCP server** | For clients without a shell: `keyshroud mcp` gives them `secrets_run`, `secrets_list`, `secrets_request`, `vault_status`. No tool ever returns a value. | | 🔗 **Committable references** | `keyshroud://item`, `bw://item`, `bw://item/username`, `bw://item/fields/name`, `bw://item/totp` in `.env.refs` files and templates: names, not values. | | ⌨️ **Paste-to-create** | New secrets go through a masked prompt in the user's terminal or a masked popup in pi — never through the chat. | | 📄 **`inject`** | Render `{{ keyshroud://… }}` and `{{ bw://… }}` templates into `0600` config files for tools that can't read env vars (`.npmrc`, kubeconfig). | | 🔎 **`scan`** | Find vault values that leaked into your working tree (pre-commit friendly): text files up to 2 MB, not `.git`, `node_modules`, `dist`, `.next`, `.venv` or links. | | ⚡ **Fast** | The local vault answers in milliseconds, offline. With Vaultwarden: one batched `bw list items` per session instead of one `bw get` (~3 s) per secret. | | 🔄 **Optional sync** | Vaultwarden on a $5 VPS or a Raspberry Pi, or Bitwarden, when the same secrets should reach several machines. `keyshroud://` and `bw://` references work side by side. | | 🧾 **Audit log** | `audit.jsonl` records which *names* were used, when, by which command. Never values. | ## Supported agents | Agent | Install | What you get | |---|---|---| | **Claude Code** | [plugin](#claude-code) | SessionStart + PostToolUse redaction hooks, skill | | **pi / omp** | [`pi install npm:keyshroud`](#pi--omp) | env hydration, `tool_result` redaction (failed calls too), `/secret` | | **Codex, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, Cursor agent** | [`npx skills add dinhkarate/keyshroud`](#other-agents-with-a-shell) | skill + CLI with masked output | | **Claude Desktop, chat-only clients** | [`mcpServers` JSON](#mcp-clients-without-a-shell) | MCP tools with masked output | | **Any shell or CI** | `keyshroud run -- ` | env injection + masked output | Agents with a shell use the CLI: it costs no tool schemas in the context, and `keyshroud run` masks output whatever the exit code. The MCP server is for clients that cannot run commands. ## Use cases **"Claude Code keeps reading my `.env`."** Run `keyshroud import` to move the values into the vault and write a `.env.refs` file with lines like `GH_TOKEN=keyshroud://myapp GH_TOKEN`, then start the agent with `keyshroud run --env-file .env.refs -- claude`. The plugin's hooks mask anything that still slips into a tool result. **"I already self-host Vaultwarden."** Log `bw` in to it and run `keyshroud doctor`: a machine with a `bw` login keeps Vaultwarden as the default, and keyshroud adds no server of its own. **"I like `op run` but don't want 1Password."** `keyshroud run` is the same idea — references in, masked output out — with the vault on your machine or on a server you host. **"My agent needs to add a new key."** It runs `keyshroud add` or calls `secrets_request` (MCP), and a hidden-input dialog pops up on your desktop; in pi it is `/secret`. You paste the value there. It never enters the chat. ## Quickstart **Requirements:** Node.js ≥ 18.19. Nothing else: no account, no server. ```bash npm install -g keyshroud # 1. Store a secret — typed into a masked prompt, never echoed. # The first one creates the local vault. keyshroud add --env GH_TOKEN --item "GitHub token" # 2. Use it keyshroud run -- gh auth status keyshroud run -- claude # start an agent with every wired secret available # 3. Check everything keyshroud doctor ``` ```console $ keyshroud add --env GH_TOKEN --item "GitHub token" Paste secret for GH_TOKEN: **************************************** keyshroud: created the local vault ~/.config/keyshroud/vault.json; its key is in the macOS keychain (keyshroud-vault-9f2c4e6a1b3d5f70), so programs running as you can open it without asking. created item=GitHub token env=GH_TOKEN targets=~/.config/keyshroud/env.json verified=yes ``` Without a terminal (an agent's shell), `add` opens a hidden-input dialog on your desktop instead, so an agent can start it and you only paste. Already have a `.env`? `keyshroud import` moves it. ### The local vault `~/.config/keyshroud/vault.json` holds every item, encrypted with AES-256-GCM under one random 256-bit key. Item names are encrypted too; the file is `0600`. Where the key lives depends on the machine: | Machine | Key | Unlocking | |---|---|---| | macOS | login keychain, entry `keyshroud-vault-` | none | | macOS with `KEYSHROUD_VAULT_KEY=secure-enclave` (or `keyshroud rekey --to secure-enclave`) | wrapped to a key in the Mac's Secure Enclave | Touch ID (or the Mac's password) when a command needs a secret; a session ends after 30 minutes | | Linux with a desktop keyring and systemd | Secret Service (`secret-tool`; found with `busctl`) | none | | Windows | DPAPI, bound to your Windows account | none | | Docker, servers, SSH with a locked keyring, Linux without systemd | derived from a passphrase (scrypt) | `keyshroud unlock`; a session ends after 30 minutes | The key mode is chosen once, when the vault is created. To be asked for a passphrase on any machine, create it with `KEYSHROUD_VAULT_KEY=passphrase keyshroud unlock` in a terminal (typed twice, at least 12 characters). When a session has ended, a command that needs a secret asks again: a masked prompt in a terminal, a dialog on the desktop, and over SSH it tells you to run `keyshroud unlock`. A Touch ID vault needs the Xcode Command Line Tools once (`xcode-select --install`): keyshroud builds a small helper from `src/touchid.swift` on first use, which takes a few seconds. The sheet appears for any caller that may ask (the CLI, `secrets_run`, Claude Code's apiKeyHelper); for this vault hooks, `status` and `doctor` never ask (with Vaultwarden they renew a session from a stored master password, which asks if you set that keychain entry to ask, and after bw has logged itself out they log in again once you approve a Touch ID sheet), and over SSH it tells you to run `keyshroud unlock` at the Mac. `keyshroud rekey` moves a vault between key types (a new key and vault id each time); run `rekey --to passphrase` before moving to another Mac. Nothing can recover a lost key or a forgotten passphrase, and the vault belongs to one machine. `vault.json` is safe to copy as long as its key is not. For backups and several machines, use Vaultwarden or Bitwarden. ### Sync across machines: Vaultwarden or Bitwarden Keep the secrets in Vaultwarden or Bitwarden instead to have them on several machines; `run`, the hooks, the MCP server and everything else work the same, through the Bitwarden CLI. **Get a vault** — pick one: - **Self-host Vaultwarden** (free, your server): follow [examples/vaultwarden](examples/vaultwarden#readme) — Docker Compose + Caddy with automatic HTTPS, from an empty VPS to `keyshroud doctor`, plus backups and hardening. - **Bitwarden cloud** (free account, no server): sign up at [bitwarden.com](https://bitwarden.com) and skip `bw config server` below (EU accounts: `bw config server https://vault.bitwarden.eu`). ```bash npm install -g @bitwarden/cli # 1. Point bw at your server and log in once bw config server https://vault.example.com bw login # 2. Make it the default for new items (keyshroud:// items keep working) mkdir -p ~/.config/keyshroud && echo bw > ~/.config/keyshroud/backend # 3. Unlock for 30 minutes (asks for the master password, which is not stored) keyshroud unlock # 4. Check everything keyshroud doctor ``` keyshroud picks the default once per machine and writes it to `~/.config/keyshroud/backend`: Vaultwarden when it finds a `bw` login or anything keyshroud 0.7 left behind, so upgrades change nothing; the local vault otherwise. `KEYSHROUD_BACKEND=local|bw` overrides it, and `keyshroud setup` switches to Vaultwarden by itself. References name their vault, so `keyshroud://…` and `bw://…` items work side by side, and `--item keyshroud://Name` or `--item bw://Name` picks one for a single item. keyshroud never stores the master password unless you do. When Vaultwarden is locked and a command needs a secret, it asks: a masked prompt in a terminal, a native dialog on the desktop (so an agent's command waits for you), and over SSH it tells you to run `keyshroud unlock`. A session ends after 30 minutes (`KEYSHROUD_SESSION_TTL_MS`): a timer runs `bw lock`, so a copied session token stops working too. On a host nobody sits at, `keyshroud unlock --unattended` asks once, in a terminal only, and opens a session without an end. To unlock without being asked, store the master password in the OS keychain (`security add-generic-password -a "$USER" -s vaultwarden-master-password -w`, or `secret-tool store` on Linux; after `setup` the entry is `keyshroud-master-password`; see the [vault setup guide](examples/vaultwarden#optional-unlock-without-being-asked)). Any program running as you can then read it, agents included. Windows has no keychain support for it. ### Least privilege: a separate agent account With the steps above, an unlocked session opens your whole Vaultwarden vault, and an agent that runs `bw` as you can use it. `setup` gives keyshroud its own `bw` login on a dedicated account instead, which holds only the secrets agents need: ```bash keyshroud setup --email you+agent@example.com # opens the signup page, then logs in with the # new master password (asked, not stored); # no `bw config server`: Bitwarden cloud keyshroud migrate # dry run: which wired items would be copied keyshroud migrate --yes # copy them; references keep working ``` - The agent login lives in `~/.config/keyshroud/bw` (`BITWARDENCLI_APPDATA_DIR`). Your own `bw` login is untouched. Its master password is not stored: keyshroud asks for it when a session ends and keeps only a scrypt hash, so `add` can refuse it as a secret. - `migrate` copies the items that wired names (and any `--env-file` / `--item`) reference, with the same names, then locks your personal vault again. Originals stay where they are. It asks for your personal master password in a terminal (or reads the keychain entry `vaultwarden-master-password`). - An agent can run `setup` too. Without a terminal it opens the signup page, where you pick the agent account's master password yourself (save it in your password manager); then the agent runs `setup --registered`, which asks for it in a dialog. The password never passes through anything the agent can read. `--confirm-unlock` and `--unattended` need a terminal. - `--confirm-unlock` (macOS) stores the master password in the keychain entry `keyshroud-master-password` so that macOS asks you before every read, i.e. every unlock. - If bw loses the login (a rejected refresh token logs it out), keyshroud on a Mac with the master password in the keychain asks for Touch ID and logs the agent account back in. - `--unattended` (hosts nobody sits at, e.g. over `ssh -t`) logs in with a session without an end. Unlock it again with `keyshroud unlock --unattended`. - Self-hosted Vaultwarden with `SIGNUPS_ALLOWED=false`: invite the address from the admin page (`/admin`), or allow signups for a minute, then pass `--registered` once the account exists. ## How it works ``` ┌──────────────────────────── your machine ─────────────────────────────┐ │ vault.json ◄── key: keychain · Secret Service · DPAPI · passphrase │ │ │ │ │ ▼ │ Vaultwarden ◄┼─bw─ keyshroud ── resolves keyshroud:// and bw:// refs ──► command's env │ (optional) │ ▲ │ │ │ └──── redactor ◄──── stdout / stderr ◄──────────────┘ │ │ │ …[文件过长——仅保留首 16KB 与末 8KB]… mits below), and a vault that fails it is never overwritten; - a local vault's passphrase is set only in a terminal and never stored; it and the Vaultwarden master password are refused as a secret, whichever vault the secret is going to; when a vault that is there cannot be asked (`bw` fails, the vault file cannot be read), nothing is stored; - env.json, auth.json and hook index writes are locked and atomic, a writer that lost its lock writes nothing, and a wired name is never overwritten without `--force`. The lock is the directory pi and omp use themselves (`.lock`, beside the file a link leads to, and beside the link too), so their writers wait for it and cannot break it (should keyshroud be killed while it holds one, pi reports the lock until the next keyshroud command clears it); - commands started by `run` and `secrets_run` never receive `BW_SESSION`, `BW_PASSWORD`, `BW_CLIENTID`, `BW_CLIENTSECRET` or `KEYSHROUD_PASSPHRASE` (these names and `BITWARDENCLI_APPDATA_DIR` cannot be wired or set by an env file either), and with `--only` the other wired names are removed from what the command inherits, so `--only` really limits what a command can read (inside pi/omp the agent process keeps the session for legacy `!bw` auth entries; its value is redacted from tool output); - two values that would get one label (``, ``) are both masked; - env files may contain only references and literals: a `!command` value is rejected, and so are variables that change what programs load or run (`PATH`, `NODE_OPTIONS`, `LD_*`, `DYLD_*`, `BASH_ENV`, `GIT_SSH_COMMAND`, …), which are also never wired or injected (the list covers the common ones, not every tool's: an env file still configures the program it is used with); - an unparseable `env.json` or `auth.json` is never overwritten. Known limits: the local vault's integrity check proves a file was sealed with its key, not that it is the latest one or who sealed it. A program that can write `vault.json` can put an older copy back, and can replace a Touch ID vault with a new one made for the same Secure Enclave key (the public half is in the file), which then opens on your next approval with its contents instead of yours; neither reveals what the vault held. The lock on pi's and omp's `auth.json` is their own (a directory, taken over after 30 s): keyshroud's writers are fenced against each other and pi cannot take over a lock keyshroud holds, but a lock that pi holds or left behind is only as safe as that scheme is between two pi processes. pi 1.5 locks beside the file a link leads to, pi 1.2 and older beside the path as it is written; keyshroud takes the first, and the second for the path it was itself given, and a write that waits there cannot land once either lock is gone. What that leaves out: an older pi that reaches `auth.json` through a different link than keyshroud does (they then share no lock at all), so point both at the same path. The locks around calls to `bw`, the unlock dialog and the local vault's session files are simpler: one is taken over when its holder shows no sign of life (30 s for the session files, 60 s for `bw`, whose holder renews it while it works; a dialog counts as open for 5 minutes and 30 s, the time it may stay on screen), so a holder that was only stalled can overlap with the next one. That can mean a second dialog, a `bw` call that fails, or a session you have to open again; it does not put a value anywhere. Claude Code's `settings.json` has no lock of its own: `claude-setup` is safe against another `claude-setup` (a stalled one replaces nothing and widens no file but the one it wrote), not against Claude Code writing the file at the same moment. The check that refuses a vault's own password as a secret asks `bw`: where no `bw` program is found, or all `bw` answers is that nobody is logged in, there is no vault on this machine to ask, and the value is stored; a `bw` that is there but does not start stops the save. A `.env.refs` can reference **any** item in your vault, not only the ones you wired, so read a cloned repo's `.env.refs` before running `--env-file` with it. `import` decides what is secret by heuristics and keeps everything else as a literal; check its plan before committing `.env.refs`. The Claude Code `PostToolUse` hook does not see failed commands (`PostToolUseFailure` cannot rewrite output) or anything a client sends as telemetry, it masks nothing until an index exists (written at session start, and added to by `run`, `secrets_run`, `get`, `inject`, `api-key`, `add`, `rotate` and `wire`; a hook that fails lets the output through as it is), and it only knows wired values, keys written into `auth.json` as plain text, and values keyshroud itself printed (`get`, `inject`, `api-key`), so a failed `keyshroud get bw://…` or `run --no-mask` still shows in the clear; run secret-using commands through `keyshroud run` or `secrets_run`, with `--only` (or `only`) naming the secrets the command needs, since every wired secret is injected otherwise. An agent with shell access as your user can open a keychain-mode local vault at any time, and use a passphrase vault's session files until the session ends. It can also read `~/.config/keyshroud/session` and use `bw` directly until that session ends — after `setup` that reaches only the agent account; a stored master password (keychain entry or `~/.config/keyshroud/master-password`) it can read at any time, which is why keyshroud asks instead by default; otherwise run agents in a sandbox or container if that matters. The same agent could also draw a window that looks like the unlock dialog; when in doubt, cancel it and run `keyshroud unlock` in a terminal. Without `setup`, keyshroud shares bw's default login, so the 30-minute lock also ends a `bw` session you opened yourself. Redaction is exact-match, so a *partial* or transformed value (`${TOKEN:0:10}`, base64, a line wrapped by a tool) is not masked. Two reshaped forms are: a value is also masked without its leading and trailing spaces or line breaks, and a value of several lines or a JSON document (a PEM key, a service account file) is also masked run by run (20 or more letters, digits and `+/=_-`), so a key shown with line numbers or as a diff stays masked; values shorter than 6 characters are not redacted (to avoid noise), so don't wire short PINs. Of the keys written into `auth.json` as plain text, one that is nothing but the name of a variable (`OPENAI_API_KEY`, `$OPENAI_API_KEY`) stands for that variable when it is set: its value is masked, the name is not (masking it would change every file that mentions the variable). A key with variables in it is masked as text and filled in as pi does, from the entry's own `env` first; the values in that `env` are not masked by themselves. And a `!command` there that is not a keyshroud reference is another program's: keyshroud does not run it to learn what it prints, so its output is masked only when the entry has a variable's name and is injected. pi's `/secret`, `/vault_add` and `/vault_rotate` popups store a pasted value without the spaces or line breaks around it; for a value where those matter, use `keyshroud add --stdin`, which keeps everything but one line break at the very end (end the input with two if the value ends with one). Report vulnerabilities privately — see [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md). ## Development ```bash npm install npm run check # typecheck + tests (fake bw, no real vault) + build node src/cli.ts doctor # run from source (Node ≥ 22.18 strips types) ``` See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md). The runtime-neutral core is in `src/core.ts` (the local vault's file format in `src/vault.ts`); agent integrations live in `extensions/`, `src/mcp.ts` and `src/hooks.ts`. ## Credits Inspired by [@jmcombs/pi-1password](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@jmcombs/pi-1password) — its popup UI and diagnostics shape are ported here (MIT). ## [0.10.11] - 2026-11-13

What the second reader found left over in 0.10.10 (review round 14), both on Windows.

### Security
- The check that refuses a vault's own password, on Windows: "there is no `bw`" now needs the
  lookup's own "not found" and a fresh search of every `PATH` directory with every `PATHEXT`
  extension that finds nothing; a place that cannot be looked into is not "nothing". A `bw` batch
  file whose `cmd.exe` cannot be started stops the save (0.10.10 took that for "no `bw`"), and a
  `bw` installed while a long-lived process runs is found.

## [0.10.10] - 2026-11-13

What the second reader found left over in 0.10.9 (review round 13).

### Security
- A key in `auth.json` with variables in it is filled in from the entry's own `env` first, then
  from the environment, as pi does; 0.10.9 looked only at the environment, so a key completed
  from the entry's `env` was not masked.
- The check that refuses a vault's own password takes "there is no `bw`" only from the start of
  `bw` itself failing for want of a file, with no file of that name anywhere a command is looked
  for. A `bw` that is there but cannot start (an unreadable shim, a missing interpreter) stops the
  save. "Nobody is logged in" counts only when it is all `bw` says.

### Changed
- The 0.10.9 note on the masking inventory said "a session the process opened"; it is a session
  the process has verified (one it was given counts too). Nothing is opened or renewed for it.

## [0.10.9] - 2026-11-13

What the second reader found left over in 0.10.8 (review round 12).

### Fixed
- 0.10.8: one entry in a wiring file that is no reference after all (`bw://Item/nosuchfield`, a
  broken `%` escape) stopped `run` and `secrets_run`, and kept the pi extension from loading, so
  pi masked nothing. Such an entry is now left out by itself; the pi extension loads and masks
  what it injects even if the rest of the inventory fails.

### Security
- The check that refuses a vault's own password: only "wrong password" from `bw`, no `bw` program,
  or `bw` answering that nobody is logged in count as "not the master password". A login that
  ran out, any other failure, or `bw` data that cannot be read now stop the save (0.10.8 took
  several of these for a "no").
- `claude-setup` gives the old file's mode to the very file it wrote, through its handle: a run
  stalled after its rename can no longer widen the file a later run put in place.
- A key in `auth.json` with variables in it is filled in exactly as pi does (a `${…}` that holds
  no name is text), so the filled-in key is masked in those cases too.
- The masking inventory reads a `bw://` reference only with a session the process opened that
  has not run out, and never opens or renews one (0.10.8 could renew a session that had ended).

### Changed
- README: a masked `!command` in pi uses the shell from your own pi settings, not one that only a
  project's settings name.

## [0.10.8] - 2026-11-13

What the second reader found left over in 0.10.7 (review round 11).

### Security
- pi: a value is now masked before pi's environment holds it, and the masking of a `!command`
  follows refreshes that come while it runs. In 0.10.7 a command started during a refresh could
  get a new value in its environment with the old masking.
- `secrets_run`: output collected up to the limit could end inside a character; the broken
  character hid the start of a secret from the cut, so that start could be shown. The incomplete
  bytes are now left out.
- Masked values that were still left out: a reference in a wiring file that an env file
  overrides under the same name; a reference under a provider's name in `auth.json`; a key with a
  variable inside it (`prefix-$NAME`), now masked both as text and with the variable filled in.
  References are read from a vault that is open (bw is not unlocked for them), and another
  program's `!command` in `auth.json` is no longer run just to learn its output.
- A value is not stored when it cannot be checked against a vault's own password: `bw` failing
  for another reason than a wrong password, or a local vault file that cannot be read, now stops
  `add` and `rotate`. A `bw lock` that fails after such a check is reported. (0.10.7 said the
  shared login "is left locked"; it was locked again only if `bw lock` worked.)
- An error from `bw` is cleaned of every place a submitted value stands in it, places that
  overlap included (replacing one value could leave the tail of the next).
- `claude-setup` writes through the same kind of lock as `auth.json`: a run that was stalled past
  its lock replaces nothing, and the new text stays `0600` until it is in place (0.10.7 gave it
  the old file's mode just before).

### Fixed
- pi: a `!command` runs in the shell set in your pi settings again (0.10.7 used pi's default).

### Changed
- README: which keys in `auth.json` are not masked (a bare variable name, another program's
  `!command`); the real times after which the simpler locks are taken over; what `--stdin` does
  with a final line break; where the password check has nothing to ask.
- The 0.10.6 note about the hook index named a warning every command gives; only `get`, `inject`
  and `api-key` give it. The 0.10.7 note about a command that cannot be started: it is reported
  with the command's name and the error code.

## [0.10.7] - 2026-11-13

What the second reader found left over in 0.10.6 (review round 10).

### Security
- The stream redactor could still let one character through in the middle of a secret that
  overlaps itself, when the output had first repeated it past the 4096 characters it may hold
  back. The cut now never goes past the place where an unfinished secret may have begun; when the
  hold is full it goes through finished secrets instead, which are masked on both sides of it.
  The same rule applies where `secrets_run` truncates long output.
- A lock beside a linked `auth.json` could be removed by a keyshroud command that had stalled
  twice, leaving a pending write that an older pi's update could then be overwritten by. The
  pending text is now named through that lock (`<link>.lock/via/…`), so it cannot land once either
  lock is gone.
- pi: the output of a `!command` is masked as it arrives, so pi shows, saves and summarizes the
  masked text (0.10.6 masked only what was sent to the model with a turn). A value stays masked
  after its name gets a new one, for tools that started before a rotation.
- Masked values that were still left out: a key in `auth.json` that an env file overrides under the
  same name; a reference that one wiring file overrides in another; a key that looks like a
  variable's name when there is no such variable; an item called `__proto__`.
- `KEYSHROUD_PASSPHRASE` can no longer be wired or set by an env file (it could be put back that
  way), and on Windows inherited names are dropped whatever their case.
- The master password of a `bw` login that keyshroud has never used (the local vault was chosen)
  is refused as a secret too; the login is left locked.
- A failed `bw create` or `bw edit` cannot quote a field of the item it was given (any of four
  characters or more), and a command that cannot be started is reported by its error code alone.
- `migrate --to local` groups references exactly as they are written: an id and a name that
  differ only in case are no longer taken for one item. References that would get one name in the
  local vault are moved only if they hold one value.
- `claude-setup` writes its backup and the new settings `0600` from the first byte, and runs one
  at a time.
- `rekey` and the first `add` keep the new key when the vault cannot be read back after a failure
  (they deleted it unless the read proved the vault was the new one).
- MCP: `only: null` is refused like any other value that is not a list; after a timeout the whole
  process group is killed even when the shell itself has gone.
- CI: the check for "generated with" lines also reads a commit's subject.

### Changed
- `secrets_run` adds the values it resolves to the hook index, and `run` does so for keys written
  out in `auth.json` as well.
- README: what the locks around `bw`, the dialog and session files do not promise; which pi
  reaches `auth.json` by which lock; what `!command` masking needs; Windows needs `/bin/sh` (WSL)
  for `!command` entries.


## [0.10.6] - 2026-11-13

A review of the whole code base (own reading and an independent one, round 9).

### Security
- pi 1.5 locks its `auth.json` beside the file a link leads to; keyshroud locked beside the path as
  it was written, so with a link anywhere in that path the two no longer excluded each other.
  keyshroud now takes the lock pi 1.5 takes (`<file>.lock` of the resolved file, where every link
  to the file meets), keeps the text of a pending write inside it, and takes the lock beside the
  link as well, for pi 1.2 and older. The separate `.keyshroud.lock` and its notes are gone.
- `run` piped through the stream redactor could let the last characters of a secret through when
  the output repeated a secret that overlaps itself (`ABCDEFABCDEF…`) for more than 4096
  characters. The stream now remembers what it let go for the length of a secret and masks one
  that began there to its end.
- Two different values that would get one label (an item named like a wired variable, say) are
  both masked now (`<redacted:NAME>`, `<redacted:NAME (2)>`); the second used to stay in the clear.
  A key written into `auth.json` as plain text is masked like a vault value, by `run`,
  `secrets_run`, pi and the hook index.
- Commands started by `run` and `secrets_run`: `BW_SESSION`, `BW_PASSWORD`, `BW_CLIENTID`,
  `BW_CLIENTSECRET` and `BITWARDENCLI_APPDATA_DIR` can no longer be wired or set by an env file
  (wiring could put back what keyshroud strips); with `--only`, the other wired names are removed
  from what the command inherits; `KEYSHROUD_PASSPHRASE` (the CI recipe) is not passed on and its
  value is masked.
- pi: the details and structured data of a tool result are masked like its text, and the output of
  a `!command` is masked in what is sent to the model. A value from Vaultwarden that keyshroud put
  into pi's environment is read again after a rotation.
- The Vaultwarden master password and the local vault's passphrase are refused as a secret in
  either vault (each was only refused in its own), also when the passphrase vault is closed.
  `migrate` skips an item holding the personal master password when that password was typed, not
  only when it came from the keychain.
- Error messages no longer quote what they were given: a failed `bw` call (the item being stored),
  unparseable hook input or settings, a command that cannot be started, a value with a NUL.
- `migrate --to local`: two references that would get one name in the local vault (a field `dsn`
  of `Sentry` and an item called `Sentry (field dsn)`) are both left where they are, and a name is
  rewired only if it still holds the reference the plan was made from.
- `claude-setup` works when there is no `settings.json` yet, keeps its backup private (`0600`,
  never over an existing file) and replaces the settings in one step.
- `rekey` no longer deletes the new keychain key when something fails after the vault was sealed
  with it.
- A first `wire` creates the configuration directory `0700` (it was the default, `0755`).
- `unwire` refuses a name that is not a variable name, so it cannot remove a provider's login from
  `auth.json`.
- MCP: `only` must be a list of names (anything else used to mean "everything"), malformed
  messages get an error instead of ending the server, and a command that ignores its timeout is
  killed after 5 more seconds.
- Calls to `bw` that reach the server: the lock between processes has an owner, is kept alive while
  held, and a waiter gives up after a minute instead of taking it over.
- CI: actions are pinned to commits, `mcp-publisher` is checked against its release digest before
  it runs, dependencies install without their scripts, a tag is published only if its commit is on
  `main` with CI green, and the check for AI attribution covers more names.

### Changed
- `wire` adds the value to the hook index at once (when the vault is open); `get`, `inject` and
  `api-key` say so when they cannot update that index (other commands do not).
- `scan` finds a value that spans lines.
- `audit.jsonl` also records `api-key` and what pi's commands add, wire and rotate.
- README: what is and is not masked in `auth.json`, what `--only` removes, the pi lock, Windows
  limits, and what "nothing is written" means for an `import` dry run.


## [0.10.5] - 2026-11-13

The last finding of the independent review (round 3, of 0.10.4).

### Security
- A keyshroud command that stalled for over 30 seconds just before replacing pi's `auth.json` could
  still overwrite what pi itself had saved meanwhile: pi broke the stale lock, wrote, and keyshroud's
  rename then landed on top. The lock keyshroud takes beside `auth.json` now holds its owner's
  token, as the vault's does, so pi (which removes a stale lock with `rmdir`) waits and then reports
  the lock instead of breaking it. A lock left by a keyshroud that was killed mid-write is cleared by
  the next keyshroud command that reads the wiring. And the new text of a write now waits inside
  that lock until it is renamed into place, so once the lock is gone, whatever removed it, a stalled
  writer has nothing left to write.

### Changed
- README: what keyshroud cannot add to the lock pi keeps on its own `auth.json`.

## [0.10.4] - 2026-11-13

Fixes from the second round of the independent review (of 0.10.3).

### Security
- After `lock`, a process that still held a passphrase or Touch ID vault in memory gave it back for a
  `vault.json` edited to name a key that needs no session and given back its size and mtime. Whether
  a session is needed is now decided by the vault the process opened, and the cached vault is used
  only for the exact bytes it was opened from (a digest, not the file's inode, size and mtime).
- A `BW_SESSION` that came with the environment (an MCP server started by a shell or by keyshroud
  that had one) was trusted for an hour, past `lock` and past the session's end. A token that is
  keyshroud's own session now ends with that session; any other is checked with bw on every use;
  the MCP server started after an update no longer gets a copy of keyshroud's session; and a failed
  unlock drops the items held in memory.
- A command that stalled for over 30 seconds could still replace `env.json`, `auth.json` or the hook
  index with what it had read before: the lock was checked before its temporary file was written,
  and not at all for the index. It is now checked once the new text is on disk, for all three.
- Two links to one `auth.json` (pi's and omp's, say) each had their own lock, so writers through both
  could drop each other's entries or temporary files. They now share a lock on the file they point to,
  and wiring a name that is already wired to the same reference is not an error.

## [0.10.3] - 2026-11-13

Fixes from an independent review of 0.10.2 (`docs/security-review-2026-11-13-astra.md`).

### Security
- After `lock` (or a session's end), a process that still held a passphrase or Touch ID vault in
  memory, such as an MCP server or pi, reopened it for session files that anyone could write: it
  checked that the files were consistent, not that they held the vault's key. A cached vault now stays
  open only under a session that holds its key, and a session that does not open the vault is removed.
- `lock` in another process did not reach a running MCP server on Vaultwarden, which went on using
  its own copy of the session and of the items for up to an hour. It now checks the session file
  before each use.
- The pi extension let a secret be wired to `NODE_OPTIONS`, `PATH` and the other variables that change
  what programs load, and injected them. Those names are now refused there and never injected.
- `inject` with two fields of one item added only the last to the hook index; two commands adding to
  the index at once could drop each other's entries. Both keep every value now.
- The Clau

ed server: those
  releases cannot log in to Vaultwarden yet (`KeyIdBackfillError`, vaultwarden#7750).

## [0.5.3] - 2026-10-15

### Security
Fixes from an independent audit and a multi-model review of 0.5.2.
- The native dialog could be used by a prompt-injected agent to phish new
  secrets, including the vault master password. It now says a program asked for
  it and warns against the master password, refuses multi-line, control or bidi
  characters and names over 120 characters, refuses a value equal to the master
  password, opens one at a time with a 30 s pause after a cancel, and is audited.
  zenity runs with `--no-markup`.
- Env files could set `PATH`, `NODE_OPTIONS`, `LD_PRELOAD` and other loader
  variables, so a cloned repo's `.env.refs` could run code. They are rejected
  in env files, refused by `add`/`wire`/`secrets_request`, and never injected.
- Streaming redaction leaked most of a secret longer than 4096 characters.
- `secrets_run` could return a partial secret when output hit the collection
  limit; the cut tail is now dropped before masking, with per-stream budgets.
- `import` missed `*_PASS`, URL passwords with no username, hex keys, and known
  key formats in names containing `PUBLIC`; `.env.refs` is now written `0600`.
- `inject -o` replaces a planted symlink instead of writing through it; temp
  files use random names and exclusive creation.

### Changed
- `add`/`rotate` read stdin only with `--stdin`; a multi-line paste into the
  `*` prompt is drained and refused instead of reaching the shell.
- `secrets_request` checks names and existing items before opening the dialog,
  reports auth.json conflicts instead of claiming success, and returns errors.
- Item names with leading or trailing spaces are refused (they shadowed
  existing items). `add`, `rotate` and `secrets_request` refresh the redact
  index and write to the audit log.

- `run` and MCP `secrets_run` strip `BW_SESSION`, `BW_PASSWORD`,
  `BW_CLIENTID` and `BW_CLIENTSECRET` from the child environment.
- Env files (`--env-file`, MCP `env_file`) reject `!command` values, including
  legacy `!bw get …` lines; auth.json still accepts them.
- `run` exits with 128+N when the child dies from signal N.
- auth.json writes refuse to replace an unparseable file, use pi's directory
  lock (`auth.json.lock/`), and write through symlinks.

### Removed
- Hard-coded server URL and personal infrastructure defaults.

### Migration from pi-vaultwarden
- Existing `!bw get password '…'` auth.json entries keep working unchanged.
- Rename `PI_VAULTWARDEN_CACHE_TTL_MS` → `KEYSHROUD_CACHE_TTL_MS`.
- Move `~/.config/pi-vaultwarden/master-password` (if used) to
  `~/.config/keyshroud/master-password`.
- Replace `pi install @piskill/pi-vaultwarden` with `pi install npm:keyshroud`.

# Security policy

## Reporting a vulnerability

Please **do not open a public issue**. Use GitHub's private vulnerability
reporting: *Security → Report a vulnerability* on
[dinhkarate/keyshroud](https://github.com/dinhkarate/keyshroud/security/advisories/new).

Include the version (`keyshroud --version`), OS, agent (Claude Code, pi, omp,
MCP client) and a minimal reproduction. Never include real secret values; use
obviously fake ones.

We aim to acknowledge reports within 3 days and to ship a fix or mitigation for
confirmed issues within 14 days, crediting reporters who want credit.

## Supported versions

Only the latest minor release receives security fixes while the project is
pre-1.0.

## Scope

In scope: any path where a secret value reaches argv, logs, diagnostics, tool or
MCP results, hook output, the audit log, files with permissions wider than
`0600`, or the model's context despite redaction being enabled; auth.json
corruption; session token exposure; a local vault that opens with the wrong key,
accepts a changed file, loses an update, or whose key or passphrase leaves the OS
key store or the user's terminal.

Note on `redact-index.json`: it holds a keyed HMAC and a 32-bit rolling hash of
each value so hooks can redact without plaintext. Anyone who can read this
`0600` file can brute-force weak values offline — the same trust boundary as the
`bw` session file next to it, which unlocks the whole vault, and as the local
vault's key in the OS keychain.

Touch ID vaults (macOS, `KEYSHROUD_VAULT_KEY=secure-enclave`): in scope is any way to open one while no
session is open without the person at the Mac approving a sheet, any key material from the helper
(`src/touchid.swift`) reaching argv, logs or errors, and a rekey or rm that changes the vault without
the approval it asks for. Out of scope: a process already running as the user that shows its own Touch
ID sheet, rewrites keyshroud, its cached helper or tools on PATH to capture the next approval, or reads
`vault.session` + `vault.token` during a session (Touch ID proves presence, not intent).

Out of scope (documented limitations, see the README's *Security model*): a
program running as the user that puts an older `vault.json` back, or replaces a
Touch ID vault with a new one made for the same Secure Enclave key (the check
proves a file was sealed with its key, not that it is the latest or whose it is); an
agent deliberately exfiltrating a value it was given (for example over the
network, or after encoding it); secrets shorter than 6 characters; values the
user prints with `get` or `env --shell` on purpose.
